sentences.text: Vegavis iaai is an extinct bird placed in the order Anseriformes and the family Vegaviidae, representing the sole species known from its genus.
The species epithet iaai honors the Argentine Antarctic Institute, the organization that leads Argentine scientific work in Antarctica.
The type locality for Vegavis geitononesos lies within the López de Bertodano Formation of Antarctica.
The species was formally described by Irazoqui and colleagues as a new taxon based on a partial skull and skeleton catalogued as MLP-PV 15-I-7-52.
Its specific name, geitononesos, commemorates the discovery of the species on Marambio Island.
The earlier Vegavis iaai specimen, catalogued as MLP 93-I-3-1, was recovered from a concretion at Cape Lamb on Vega Island in 1992.
Because the fossil was embedded in a hard matrix, it was not described until 2005 after careful preparation.
The specimen now resides in the Museo de La Plata in Argentina, where computed axial tomography scans have been employed to visualize its bone structure without damaging the delicate remains.
A high metabolic rate would have enabled Vegavis to cope with the cold, high-latitude environment of Antarctic Maastrichtian ecosystems.
The bones display osteosclerosis, a condition of increased bone density also observed in the contemporary bird Polarornis, suggesting adaptation to a marine or diving lifestyle.
Vegavis belongs to the clade Anseriformes, the group that includes modern waterfowl.
Among living birds it is most closely related to the family Anatidae, which contains ducks and geese, though it is not regarded as a direct ancestor of that family.
Vegavis lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, specifically in the uppermost part of that interval.
This places the bird roughly 65 million years ago in Antarctica, a time when the continent was situated at high southern latitudes.
The genus persisted from about 72.2 to 66 million years ago, spanning the latter portion of the Maastrichtian.

Researchers note that the palatine bone of Vegavis combines primitive features with unique characters within the broader group Neognathae, a pattern that fuels ongoing discussion about its precise evolutionary relationships.
